title: Pashupati, who loosens the rope
hookLine: the lord of creatures once roamed as a deer, and in Shaiva teaching he's the one who unties the soul
carry: pati, pashu, pasha: the lord unties the soul
tomorrow: what did Vishnu offer when one lotus was missing?

cards: Kathmandu, early morning, beside the Bagmati river. Monkeys run along the temple walls. Pilgrims queue with marigolds, and a little way down the bank, smoke rises from the cremation ghats.
The temple is Pashupatinath, and the name over its door is one of Shiva's: Pashupati. The animals in the courtyard are a fitting welcome, because the name is about them, and then about everyone.

teach.b: Pashupati joins two words. Pati is lord. Pashu is a creature, the kind tied up in a yard: a cow, a goat.
So at its simplest, Pashupati is the lord of animals, who looks after every living thing. A legend told in Nepal goes further.

teach.h: THE LORD WHO ROAMED AS A DEER.
teach.b: Shiva once left his mountain for the forest by the Bagmati, and there he roamed as a deer among the animals. The gods searched until they found him and caught him by the horn.
The horn broke, and the piece left behind came to be worshipped where the temple stands. The lord of creatures had been one of them.

Shaiva teachers then turned the name into a whole teaching, in schools such as Shaiva Siddhanta. Pati, the lord, is Shiva. Pashu is every soul, you and me included, called a creature because it's tied.
And pasha is the rope. Teachers name its strands: a root ignorance that makes the soul feel small, the pull of past actions, and the hold of the changing world.
And here is the Shaiva heart of it: the creature can't simply cut its own rope.

teach.h: PATI, PASHU, PASHA: LORD, SOUL, ROPE.
teach.b: The soul does its practice, and the lord loosens the rope, by grace.

teach.h: THE LORD LOOSENS IT, BY GRACE.
teach.b: Humbling, because it puts everyone in the yard with the goats.
Hopeful, because a rope can be untied, and someone is untying it. So when an old anger or a habit holds you like a tether, a Shaiva devotee doesn't just grit their teeth.
They keep up the practice, and they ask Pashupati to loosen what they can't.

how: Shiva is worshipped as Pashupati at the Pashupatinath temple on the Bagmati river in Kathmandu, where a local legend tells of Shiva roaming as a deer; Shaiva Siddhanta teachers explain their path through pati, pashu and pasha: the lord, the soul and the bond, loosened by the lord's grace. Names such as Om Pashupataye Namah are offered one by one in temple archana.

o: a temple hymn sung to bless the cattle at harvest
a Nepali festival where tied animals are set free
a hymn of Shiva's names, here the lord who loosens the rope

games.q: pati, pashu, pasha — tap the pairs.

s: Pashupati only ever meant lord of cattle
it means lord of creatures, and Shaiva teachers read pashu as every soul.
in Shaiva Siddhanta, pasha is the rope that ties the soul
a root ignorance, the pull of past actions, the hold of the changing world.
in Shaiva Siddhanta, the soul cuts its own rope with willpower alone
the soul does its practice, and the lord loosens the rope by grace.

games.q: a teacher calls you a pashu, a tied-up creature in the yard. how might a Shaiva teacher mean it?
o: as an insult: you're no better than a goat.
as a diagnosis: you're tied, and the rope can be loosened.
as a compliment: animals are simple.
games.why: in Shaiva teaching every soul is a pashu, tied by pasha, and Pashupati is the lord who loosens the rope.

practice: Ask quietly what's pulling at you today, a worry, a habit, a grudge, and feel where it tugs: the chest, the belly, the hands.
If you pray, offer it the way names are offered in a temple: say Om Pashupataye Namah, I bow to the lord of creatures, slowly, eleven times, and on each one hand the knot to Shiva to loosen.
If you'd like, set a flower or a little water before an image of him. If you don't pray, on each out-breath let the rope go a little slack, the way you'd loosen a knot without cutting it.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Pashupati, lord of every creature, and in Shaiva teaching, the lord who loosens the soul's rope by grace.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Pashupati, lord (pati) of creatures (pashu); a name of Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: pati, pashu, pasha: the lord unties the soul. A rope can be loosened. A week, done.
